title: What Is Oxidation in Wine?
description: Learn how oxygen can help or harm wine, how oxidation tastes and smells, and when oxidative character is intentional rather than a fault.
text: Topic: Wine oxidation Highlights Oxidation happens when wine compounds react with oxygen over time. Unwanted oxidation can make wine seem dull, flat, tired or brown. Possible aromas include bruised apple, nuts, cardboard, straw or hay. Oxidation is not always a fault: some wines are deliberately made in an oxidative style. One smell or a change in colour does not prove that a wine is oxidised. Resealing an opened bottle, limiting air exposure and avoiding heat can slow further change. Chilling may slow oxidation, but it cannot reverse established chemical changes. Oxidation is different from cork taint, reduction and volatile acidity. Quick Answer Oxidation in wine is a group of chemical changes caused by wine’s exposure to oxygen. Over time, oxygen can change a wine’s colour, aroma, flavour and sense of freshness. Unwanted oxidation may mute fresh fruit and floral aromas, make the wine taste flat or tired, and produce notes such as bruised apple, nuts, cardboard, straw, hay or sherry. White wines may become noticeably darker or browner, while red wines can lose bright fruit and develop a browner, more developed appearance. But oxidation is not automatically a fault. Winemakers sometimes manage oxygen deliberately to create a particular style. Nutty, dried-fruit, caramelised or sherry-like characters can be desirable in some fortified or traditionally matured wines. The important question is whether the change suits the wine’s intended style. You cannot diagnose oxidation with certainty from one smell, one flavour or colour alone. Normal ageing, heat damage and other wine faults can overlap with some of the same signs. What Does Oxidation Change? Wine contains many compounds that can react with oxygen. These reactions may alter: Aroma: Fresh fruit and floral notes may fade, replaced by more developed, nutty or stale characters. Flavour: The wine may lose brightness and seem dull, tired or flat. Colour: Pale wines can shift towards yellow, amber or brown. Red wines may become browner or brick-like as they develop. Freshness: The wine may feel less lively, with a shorter or less energetic finish. Structure: Oxygen-related reactions can change how a wine’s phenolic compounds and other components are perceived. The chemistry is more complicated than oxygen simply “turning alcohol into acetaldehyde”. Acetaldehyde is associated with oxidation, but several compounds and reactions contribute to the overall result. How Can You Recognise Possible Oxidation? Treat the following as clues rather than a diagnosis. White wine An oxidised white wine may show less floral or fresh-fruit aroma, along with bruised apple, nuts, cardboard, straw or hay. Its colour may become noticeably darker, amber or brown. On the palate, it may seem tired or lacking in freshness. Rosé Rosé may lose its fresh red-fruit and floral character. Its pink colour can look duller or move towards orange or brown, and the wine may seem less bright. Red wine An affected red may lose fresh berry aromas and develop dried-fruit, nutty or stale characters. Its colour may become browner, and the palate may seem less lively. Red wine is not immune to oxidation; its higher phenolic content can simply influence how the changes develop. Sparkling wine Sparkling wine may lose freshness and aromatic precision. Other storage or age-related changes can occur at the same time, so a flat or less lively bottle should not automatically be labelled oxidised. Fortified and oxidative styles A nutty, dried-fruit or sherry-like character may be intentional in some fortified or oxidative wines. The same descriptor can be welcome in one wine and a fault in another. How Does Oxygen Get Into Wine? Oxygen exposure can happen at several points: during crushing, pressing and other winemaking operations; during pumping, transfers, racking or filtration; through exposed tank or barrel headspace; during bottling and packaging; through or around the closure; during transport or storage; after the bottle is opened. In a packaged bottle, oxygen may be dissolved in the wine, present in the space above the wine—called the headspace or ullage —or associated with the closure. Once you open a bottle, air enters and the headspace can become an important source of further oxygen exposure. Time and temperature matter too. Warm storage can speed chemical change, while a longer period of oxygen contact gives those changes more opportunity to develop. Wine composition also matters: phenolics, sulphur dioxide, acidity and other characteristics influence how a particular wine responds. Is Oxidation Always a Fault? No. Some winemakers deliberately use or accept oxygen exposure to shape a wine’s character. Certain fortified and traditionally matured wines may be expected to show developed, nutty, dried-fruit or caramelised notes. In those wines, oxidative character can be part of the style rather than a defect. Oxidation becomes unwanted when it damages the qualities the wine was meant to preserve. For example, losing the fresh fruit and floral character of a young aromatic white may be considered a fault, while similar developed notes may be appropriate in a deliberately oxidative wine. So “oxidative” can describe a winemaking or maturation direction, while “oxidised” often describes an unwanted condition. Context matters. How Can You Slow Unwanted Oxidation? After opening a bottle: reseal it promptly; minimise repeated opening and unnecessary agitation; keep it in a cool, stable place; avoid prolonged exposure to direct sun, hot rooms, cars, garages and sheds; reduce the amount of air above the wine where practical. For Australian households, heat is especially worth considering during warm weather. A bottle left in a hot car or shed can change more quickly than one kept in stable, moderate conditions. There is no universal opened-bottle time limit that applies equally to every wine. Refrigeration can slow many chemical reactions and is a useful practical step, particularly for white, rosé and sparkling wine. However, cooling does not remove oxygen already absorbed by the wine and does not restore freshness that has already been lost. Screw caps and cork closures manage oxygen differently. Screw caps often provide consistent, low oxygen transmission, while natural cork performance varies. Neither closure should be described as universally superior: closure design, bottling conditions, the wine itself and storage all influence the result. Can You Fix an Oxidised Wine? Usually, not at home. Resealing and cooling can slow further change, but they cannot generally reverse established chemical oxidation. Once aroma compounds have changed and freshness has been lost, putting the wine in the fridge will not return it to its original condition. Aerating or decanting is not a reliable cure. Air may help some wines open up, but it adds oxygen and could make an already oxidised wine decline further. If a wine seems unexpectedly changed, compare it with another bottle of the same wine if possible. A single brown colour, nutty aroma or tired flavour is not conclusive proof, but a combination of signs can suggest that the wine has not travelled or been stored as intended. Oxidation Compared With Other Wine Problems Cork taint: Often associated with musty, mouldy, damp-cardboard or wet-newspaper aromas. It is not the same as oxidation. Reduction: More commonly associated with sulphury, struck-match, rubber, cabbage or rotten-egg characters. It is not simply the opposite smell of oxidation. Volatile acidity: Can produce vinegar, acetic or nail-polish-remover notes. Oxygen may support some related microbial activity, but volatile acidity is a separate condition. Brettanomyces: A yeast-related condition that can contribute farmyard, leather, medicinal or smoky characters. Heat damage: May produce cooked, stewed or jammy fruit and can accelerate other changes, but heat damage is not identical to oxidation. Normal ageing: A wine can develop savoury or tertiary characters as it matures without being faulty. Sediment: A physical deposit in the bottle, not evidence of oxidation. Wine faults can overlap, so sensory impressions are useful clues rather than laboratory proof. Frequently Asked Questions Is oxidised wine unsafe to drink? Oxidation is primarily a quality and flavour issue. It can make wine unpleasant, but an oxidised taste does not by itself prove that a wine is unsafe. If the wine appears contaminated, has an unusual physical problem or seems otherwise suspect, do not drink it. Does brown wine always mean oxidation? No. Browning can be a clue, especially in a pale wine, but colour is affected by grape variety, production, age and style. Taste and aroma matter too. Does opening a bottle immediately oxidise it? Opening introduces air, but noticeable change depends on the wine, the amount of oxygen, temperature, time and other factors. Opening does not mean every wine is instantly oxidised. Is oxidation the same as ageing? No. Ageing can involve oxygen-related development, but a mature wine is not automatically oxidised or faulty. Whether a developed character is desirable depends on the wine’s style and condition. Can decanting prevent oxidation? No. Decanting increases the wine’s contact with air. It may help some young or closed wines express themselves, but it is not a treatment for unwanted oxidation. Related Learning What is wine? How wine is made What is fortified wine? Winemaking

title: What Is Pinot Gris / Pinot Grigio?
description: Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are names for the same grape. Learn why both appear on labels, how the styles can differ and what Australian drinkers should look for.
text: Highlights Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are two names for the same white-wine grape variety . Pinot Gris is the French name; Pinot Grigio is the Italian name. The grape has greyish-pink or dusky skins, but it is normally made into white wine. Pinot Grigio is often associated with light, crisp and fresh wines. Pinot Gris is often associated with riper, fuller and more textured wines. Those style associations are tendencies, not rules. Australian producers may use either name for different styles. Climate, harvest timing and winemaking choices can matter more than the name on the front label. Quick Answer Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are names for the same grape variety. “Pinot Gris” is French, while “Pinot Grigio” is Italian. Both names refer to the grape’s greyish or dusky skin colour. The variety is usually made as a dry white wine. Depending on where it is grown and how it is made, it can be light, crisp and citrusy, or fuller, riper and more textured. Common flavours include apple, pear, citrus and stone fruit, with some wines showing mineral, spice, creamy or lightly savoury notes. The names can offer a useful clue to style. Pinot Grigio is often linked with earlier-picked, fresh and energetic wines, while Pinot Gris is often linked with riper and more substantial expressions. But this is not a universal rule. In Australia, a producer may use either name for a crisp, rich or textural wine. If you are choosing a bottle, treat “Gris” or “Grigio” as a starting point. Then read the rest of the label or producer description for clues such as crisp , dry , fresh , textured , lees-aged , barrel-fermented or off-dry . One Grape, Two Names The simplest way to understand Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio is to think of them as two languages describing the same grape. Pinot Gris is the French name. Pinot Grigio is the Italian name. Gris and grigio both mean “grey”. The grape’s ripe skins can have a greyish-pink, dusky or coppery appearance. Despite this colour, Pinot Gris/Grigio is normally made into white wine. Grape skin colour does not automatically determine whether a finished wine is red or white; winemaking choices, especially the amount of skin contact, also matter. Pinot Gris belongs to the Pinot family and is related to Pinot Noir. The word “Pinot” is associated with the pine-cone-like shape of Pinot-family grape bunches. Text-first learning component: Same grape, two names Pinot Gris = Pinot Grigio French name | Italian name | same grape variety Do Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio Taste Different? They can, but not because they are different grapes. Over time, the names have developed broad stylistic associations. A wine labelled Pinot Grigio is often expected to be: light to medium-bodied; fresh and crisp; high in perceived acidity; citrusy, mineral or green-apple driven; clean and refreshing. A wine labelled Pinot Gris is often expected to be: riper and fuller; broader or rounder in texture; flavoured with pear, ripe apple or stone fruit; silky, creamy or lightly spicy; sometimes influenced by lees contact, skin contact or oak. These are useful traditions, but they are not fixed definitions. A Pinot Gris can be bright and delicate, while a Pinot Grigio can be rich or textural. The producer, region, vintage and winemaking decisions all matter. That is why it is better to think of Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio as a style spectrum , rather than two sealed categories. Style spectrum: crisp and light → rounded and textured → rich and luscious The label name alone does not determine where a wine sits. What Does Pinot Gris / Pinot Grigio Taste Like? There is no single Pinot Gris or Pinot Grigio flavour profile. The wine may show: lemon or other citrus; green apple; pear; peach or other stone fruit; floral notes; mineral or stony impressions; spice; creamy or savoury texture. Lighter examples are usually driven by freshness. They may feel lean, clean and mouth-watering, with fruit and mineral notes rather than obvious oak. Fuller examples may feel broader and softer. Riper fruit, lees contact, skin contact or barrel fermentation can add weight and texture. Some wines may have a silky or creamy impression even when they are still dry. Is Pinot Gris sweet? Most table-wine examples are dry, but the wine can taste fruity or luscious. A ripe pear flavour is not the same as sweetness from residual sugar. Residual sugar is the sugar left in a wine after fermentation. It can make a wine taste sweet, while fruit ripeness, alcohol and texture can make a dry wine seem rich or soft. If sweetness matters to you, look for terms such as dry , off-dry or sweet , and check the producer’s description where available. Why Do Styles Vary? The same grape can produce noticeably different wines because several decisions shape the finished style. Climate and site Cooler conditions can help a vineyard retain acidity and freshness. Warmer or riper conditions can contribute more body, fruit weight and richness. This is a broad tendency, not a formula: vineyard site, season and picking decisions also matter. Harvest timing Earlier picking generally preserves freshness and lighter fruit character. Later picking can bring more ripeness, concentration and texture. This is one reason the classic light Grigio and fuller Gris associations developed. Skin contact Allowing grape juice to remain in contact with the skins can influence colour, texture and phenolic feel. In Pinot Gris/Grigio, it may contribute a deeper colour or a more textured, savoury style. Lees contact Lees are the sediment left after fermentation, including yeast cells. Keeping wine on its lees can contribute breadth, creaminess or a more rounded texture. Fermentation vessel and oak Stainless steel is often used when a winemaker wants to preserve freshness and fruit character. Barrel fermentation or oak maturation may add texture, spice, toast or vanilla. Oak is optional, not a defining feature of Pinot Gris. Style-influence flow: climate + harvest timing + ripeness + skin contact + lees + oak → final wine style Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio in Australia Australian drinkers may see both names on domestic and imported labels. Pinot Grigio is common on imported Italian wines, while Australian producers may choose either Pinot Gris or Pinot Grigio for their own wines. Australia does not have one universal “Gris style” and one universal “Grigio style”. A bottle’s name can suggest an intention, but it does not guarantee the flavour or texture inside. Relevant Australian contexts include cool or maritime regions such as: Mornington Peninsula; Tasmania; Adelaide Hills; Yarra Valley; Orange. Wine Australia identifies Pinot Gris/Grigio as an important variety in the Mornington Peninsula, where it describes examples as medium-bodied, fruit-driven and mineral in character. These descriptions are broad regional tendencies, not rules for every bottle. Australia also produces Pinot Gris/Grigio in larger inland regions, so the category is not limited to one type of climate or one premium style. Wine Australia’s 2024 variety snapshot recorded 70,757 tonnes crushed in 2024 , while its planting figure of 3,731 hectares used 2015 data. These figures are dated and are not necessary for choosing a bottle, but they illustrate that the variety is established across Australian wine production. How to Choose a Bottle If you prefer a fresh, easy-drinking white, look for descriptions such as: crisp; fresh; bright; mineral; citrusy; light-bodied. If you prefer more weight or texture, look for: ripe pear or stone fruit; rounded; creamy; textured; lees-aged; barrel-fermented; skin contact. Do not assume that “Pinot Gris” automatically means rich or that “Pinot Grigio” automatically means simple and crisp. The producer description, region, vintage and technical notes can give you a better idea of the wine’s style. Serving and Food Pinot Gris/Grigio is generally served chilled. Avoid serving it so cold that its aromas and texture disappear. Crisper styles can work well with seafood, shellfish, salads and lighter dishes. Fuller examples may suit richer seafood, poultry or lightly spiced food. These are starting points rather than strict pairing rules; match the food to the wine’s body, acidity and texture. The Bottom Line Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are two names for the same grape. The names come from French and Italian usage and can suggest different stylistic traditions, but neither name guarantees a particular flavour. Expect anything from a light, crisp and citrus-driven white to a fuller wine with ripe fruit and a more rounded texture. For the most reliable guide, read beyond the grape name and look for the producer’s description of the wine’s freshness, sweetness and texture.

title: What Is Pinot Noir?
description: Pinot Noir is a red grape variety known for fresh acidity, red-fruit flavours and often lighter to medium-bodied wines. Learn what it tastes like, whether it is sweet and where it is grown in Australia.
text: Highlights Pinot Noir is a red grape variety and the name of the wine made from it. It commonly produces light- to medium-bodied red wines , although some examples are fuller and more concentrated. Typical flavours include cherry, strawberry, raspberry, floral, earthy and savoury notes . Pinot Noir usually has fresh acidity and fine to moderate tannin. Most still Pinot Noir is dry , even when it tastes strongly of ripe fruit. Australian Pinot Noir is especially associated with cooler regions , including Tasmania, the Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula and Adelaide Hills. Pinot Noir can be delicate and silky, but it is not automatically pale, weak, sweet or simple. Quick answer Pinot Noir is a dark-skinned wine grape variety used mainly to make red wine. The name “Pinot Noir” can refer to the grape itself or to a bottle of wine made primarily from that grape. Most Pinot Noir is red, dry and light to medium bodied. It often has noticeable acidity, relatively fine tannin and red-fruit flavours such as cherry, strawberry and raspberry. Depending on where it was grown and how it was made, it may also show floral, earthy, savoury or spicy notes. Pinot Noir is strongly associated with cool or temperate climates. In Australia, important examples come from Tasmania, Victoria and South Australia, including the Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula and Adelaide Hills. The most useful thing to remember is that Pinot Noir is a variety with a broad range of styles—not a single fixed flavour formula. One bottle may be pale, bright and silky; another may be darker, richer and firmer. What kind of wine is Pinot Noir? Pinot Noir is a red grape variety. Its name is also commonly used for the still red wine made from it. It is not a region, a brand or a description of sweetness. A wine labelled Pinot Noir tells you primarily which grape variety has been used. Pinot Noir is also an important grape in traditional-method sparkling wine, including Australian sparkling wine. However, when people casually ask for “a Pinot Noir”, they usually mean a still red wine. Compared with deeply coloured varieties such as Shiraz or Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir often produces a paler red wine. Its colour can range from relatively light ruby to deeper ruby or garnet, depending on ripeness, extraction, vintage and winemaking. What does Pinot Noir taste like? Pinot Noir may show flavours such as: cherry; strawberry; raspberry and other red berries; plum in some examples; floral aromas; earthy or forest-floor notes; savoury or spice characters. Cherry and strawberry are common descriptions, but they are not guarantees. Pinot Noir does not always taste earthy, and it does not always taste delicate or fruity. A wine’s flavour depends on its climate, vineyard site, vintage, ripeness and winemaking. The same grape variety can therefore produce noticeably different wines from one region—or even one vineyard—to another. When tasting Pinot Noir, you might notice a lighter texture and red-fruit freshness in one wine, then more concentration, darker fruit or firmer structure in another. Neither style is automatically more “correct”. Is Pinot Noir sweet? Most still Pinot Noir is made as a dry red wine. That does not mean it will taste completely unsweet. Cherry, strawberry and raspberry flavours can create a juicy or sweet-fruited impression even when the wine contains little residual sugar. This is an important distinction: Sweetness refers to sugar in the wine. Fruit flavour describes the aromas and flavours you perceive. A dry Pinot Noir can smell and taste strongly of ripe strawberries without being a sweet wine. Is Pinot Noir light-bodied? Pinot Noir is often light to medium bodied, meaning it may feel less weighty or rich than a full-bodied red such as a powerful Shiraz or Cabernet Sauvignon. But “light-bodied” does not mean thin, weak or low quality. Pinot Noir can have plenty of flavour and concentration while still feeling relatively graceful in the mouth. Some examples are fuller and firmer, particularly when made from riper fruit or through winemaking choices that build texture and body. A useful beginner summary is: Feature Common Pinot Noir tendency Colour Pale to medium ruby, though variation is considerable Body Often light to medium Acidity Usually fresh and noticeable Tannin Often fine or moderate, but variable Fruit character Commonly red-fruited Texture Delicate and silky to concentrated and firm Sweetness Most still examples are dry These are broad tendencies, not rules for every bottle. Why does Pinot Noir taste different from bottle to bottle? Several factors shape the final wine. Climate Pinot Noir is commonly associated with cool or temperate climates. Cooler conditions can help preserve acidity and red-fruit freshness, while warmer conditions may encourage riper fruit, more body and higher alcohol. That is only a general tendency. Climate does not guarantee a particular colour, alcohol level or body. Vineyard site Elevation, aspect, proximity to water, soils and drainage can affect how quickly grapes ripen and how much water the vines receive. These differences help explain why Pinot Noir can vary within the same broad region. Vintage A growing season may be warmer, cooler, wetter or drier than another. Vintage conditions influence ripeness, acidity, concentration and the decisions made at harvest. Ripeness and harvest timing Picking earlier or later can change the balance between acidity, fruit character, alcohol and texture. Winemakers must decide what style they want from the fruit. Winemaking Techniques such as whole-bunch use, fermentation temperature, extraction, oak and maturation can alter aroma, tannin and texture. They are choices, not requirements for making “real” Pinot Noir. Oak is also not a defining feature of every Pinot Noir. Some winemakers use it to add texture or spice, while others use less new oak so the fruit remains more prominent. Pinot Noir in Australia Australia’s Pinot Noir identity is closely connected with cooler or temperate growing regions. Tasmania, parts of Victoria and the Adelaide Hills are important contexts for the variety. Australian Pinot Noir is not one uniform style. Research comparing wines from regions including Tasmania, the Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula and Adelaide Hills found regional differences in chemical and sensory composition. These differences are useful evidence that place matters, but they do not mean every wine from a region tastes the same. Tasmania Tasmania is one of Australia’s major Pinot Noir regions. Its island position and Southern Ocean influence contribute to a cool climate, while long, sunny and dry autumns can help grapes ripen and develop flavour. Tasmanian Pinot Noir may be light to medium bodied, with red apple, cherry and strawberry characters. Tasmania contains several distinct growing areas, so these descriptions are broad tendencies rather than a tasting rule. Yarra Valley Pinot Noir is the Yarra Valley’s most planted and important grape variety. Differences in elevation and aspect contribute to a range of regional expressions. Yarra Valley Pinot Noir may show cherry, strawberry and plum characters. Some wines are bright and delicate, while others have greater concentration and structure. Mornington Peninsula The Mornington Peninsula is strongly associated with Pinot Noir. Bass Strait, Port Phillip Bay and Western Port contribute maritime influences, while local differences in elevation, aspect and soils create variation across the region. Typical descriptions include strawberry and cherry fruit, fresh acidity and fine tannin. As elsewhere, these are general tendencies rather than a promise about every bottle. Adelaide Hills The Adelaide Hills is an important South Australian region for Pinot Noir. Its cooler conditions also make some fruit suitable for traditional-method sparkling wine. Still red examples may be medium bodied, with ripe cherry and berry characters. The region’s Pinot Noir should not be treated as identical to Tasmanian, Yarra Valley or Mornington Peninsula examples. For more regional detail, see the WineDaddy guides to the Yarra Valley and Mornington Peninsula . What food goes with Pinot Noir? Pinot Noir’s acidity, red-fruit character and often moderate tannin can make it a flexible food wine. Approachable matches include: roast chicken; pork; salmon; mushrooms; charcuterie; pâté and terrines. These are suggestions, not rules. A fuller Pinot Noir may work with richer food, while a lighter and brighter example may suit simpler dishes. Pinot Noir is generally more enjoyable slightly cool than warm. Avoid serving it overheated, which can make the alcohol feel more obvious and the wine less fresh. Can Pinot Noir age? Some high-quality Pinot Noir can develop with age. Wine Australia notes that the very best examples may age for 10–15 years. That does not mean every Pinot Noir should be cellared. Many bottles are made to be enjoyed while their fresh fruit is prominent. Ageing potential depends on the individual wine, vintage, producer and storage conditions. A final way to think about Pinot Noir Pinot Noir is often described as elegant, silky or delicate, but those words describe only part of its range. It can be light or more concentrated, fruit-driven or savoury, pale or relatively dark, and immediately approachable or capable of developing with age. The common thread is the grape variety—not one compulsory style. If you want deeper information about Pinot Noir’s history, taxonomy, clones, viticulture and technical winemaking, continue to the WineDaddy Pinot Noir grape profile . Related Learning What is wine? title: What Is Riesling? A Beginner’s Guide to This Aromatic White Wine
description: Riesling is an aromatic white grape that can make dry, off-dry and sweet wines. Learn how acidity, fruitiness and Australian regions shape its style.
text: Highlights Riesling is a white grape variety, not a single sweetness level. It is often aromatic, light- to medium-bodied and high in acidity. Common flavours include lime, lemon, green apple, peach and floral notes. Riesling can be bone-dry, off-dry, sweet or occasionally sparkling. Most Australian Riesling is made in a crisp, dry style. Clare Valley and Eden Valley are important Australian examples, but Riesling is grown in many regions. Some Rieslings can age and develop honeyed, toasty or nutty flavours. Quick answer: what is Riesling? Riesling is a white wine grape variety. The name is also commonly used for wines made primarily from that grape. Riesling is best known for its lively acidity and fragrant character. A young Riesling may smell or taste of lime, lemon, green apple, peach or flowers. Those flavours can appear in a completely dry wine, so Riesling is not automatically sweet. The grape can produce several styles, from bone-dry to off-dry, sweet and dessert wines. In Australia, Riesling is especially associated with crisp, dry wines from regions such as Clare Valley and Eden Valley, although Tasmania, Great Southern, Canberra District and other regions also produce it. The most useful beginner lesson is simple: the word “Riesling” tells you the grape, but not necessarily how sweet the finished wine will be. What does Riesling taste like? Young Riesling is often light- to medium-bodied, fresh and aromatic. Common descriptions include: lime and lemon; green apple; peach; citrus blossom or other floral notes; a clean, mouth-watering finish. These are typical possibilities rather than a fixed checklist. Climate, ripeness, region, winemaking and bottle age all influence the final wine. Riesling’s acidity is one of its defining features. Acidity creates freshness and makes your mouth water, rather like the sensation from biting into a crisp green apple. It can also balance residual sugar, allowing a wine to be sweet without feeling heavy. Riesling is therefore a useful variety for understanding the difference between fruitiness , sweetness , acidity and body : Fruitiness describes aromas and flavours. Sweetness mainly comes from residual sugar left in the wine. Acidity provides freshness and structure. Body describes how light or full the wine feels in your mouth. A wine can smell of ripe peach and still be dry. Another can contain some residual sugar but remain fresh because of its acidity. Is Riesling sweet? Not necessarily. Most Australian Riesling is dry, meaning it contains little perceptible residual sugar. It can still taste intensely of citrus, apple or flowers. Riesling is also made in off-dry, sweet and dessert styles. Off-dry wines contain some residual sugar but may taste balanced rather than obviously sweet. Sweeter styles can be made by harvesting grapes later or by retaining some of the grape’s sugar during fermentation. When choosing a bottle, look for words such as: dry ; off-dry ; sweet ; late harvest ; dessert wine . The grape name alone is not a reliable sweetness guide. If the label is unclear, the producer’s description or a retailer’s tasting note may provide more useful information. For a broader explanation of sweetness, see what is sweet wine? . Why can Riesling taste so different from bottle to bottle? Riesling’s final style is shaped by a chain of decisions and conditions: Climate and site → ripeness and acidity → harvest timing → fermentation and maturation → finished wine. Cooler conditions can help the grapes retain acidity and aromatic freshness. Warmer conditions may encourage riper fruit and a broader texture, although no climate produces exactly one style. Vintage conditions, vineyard site and harvest decisions matter as well. The winemaker’s choices also influence the result. Cool, temperature-controlled fermentation in stainless steel is common for Australian Riesling because it helps preserve fresh fruit and aromatic purity. New oak is not common, although some producers use lees ageing, skin contact or alternative vessels to add texture. Many Australian Rieslings are bottled relatively early to preserve their bright, direct character. A screwcap, also called a Stelvin closure, is very common for Australian Riesling. It can help limit oxygen exposure and preserve freshness, but it is not a guarantee of quality or a particular style. Can Riesling age? Some Rieslings can age very well. Their acidity provides a firm structure that can help the wine remain fresh as it develops. Young Riesling tends to emphasise citrus, apple and floral characters. With bottle age, some examples develop honeyed, lemon-curd, nutty or toasty notes. A distinctive petroleum-like character may also appear in some aged Rieslings, although it is not present in every bottle and is not, by itself, proof that a wine is faulty or superior. Ageing potential varies with the wine, vintage, sweetness, acidity, closure and storage conditions. Not every bottle needs to be cellared, and ageing is not a requirement for enjoying Riesling. Australian Riesling Riesling has an established place in Australian wine. It is grown in several parts of the country and is particularly associated with dry, cool-climate styles. Clare Valley Clare Valley is one of Australia’s major Riesling regions. Wines from the region are often associated with bright acidity, light body and lime or citrus flavours. Some can be enjoyed young, while well-made examples may also develop complexity with age. Eden Valley Eden Valley, within the Barossa Zone, is another important Australian Riesling region. Its elevated vineyard sites are associated with lemon and lime characters, fresh acidity and a steely finish. “Mineral” is sometimes used as a tasting description for these wines; it should not be read as proof that minerals from the soil directly enter the wine and create a specific flavour. Other regions Riesling is also produced in Tasmania, Great Southern, Canberra District, Langhorne Creek, Padthaway, the Riverland and other Australian regions. These examples show why Australian Riesling should not be reduced to one regional style. You can explore broader Australian wine geography through the Australian regions index. Detailed guides to individual Riesling regions may be covered separately. How should a beginner choose a Riesling? Start with the style you want rather than assuming all Riesling tastes the same. For a crisp, refreshing wine, look for an Australian dry Riesling, particularly from a cool-climate region. For a softer or fruitier impression, look for an off-dry description. For dessert or a richer occasion, look for a sweet or late-harvest style. For a more developed experience, look for a bottle with some age, remembering that older does not automatically mean better. A regional name can offer a clue, but it is not a guarantee. The vintage, producer description and stated sweetness style can tell you more. Riesling is usually served chilled. Dry examples can work well with oysters, shellfish, lighter fish, salads and goat’s cheese. Off-dry or sweeter examples may suit spicy dishes, pâté or soft cheese. These are starting points, not rules. Frequently asked questions Is Riesling a white wine? Yes. Riesling is a white grape variety used to make white wines. Is Riesling always dry? No. Most Australian Riesling is dry, but the variety can also produce off-dry, sweet, dessert and occasionally sparkling wines. Is Riesling a sweet wine? It can be, but the grape name does not determine sweetness. Check the label or producer description for clues. What is the difference between Riesling and other white wines? Riesling is commonly recognised for its pronounced acidity and aromatic citrus, apple, peach and floral characters. Its style can still vary considerably with climate, ripeness, winemaking and age. Is Riesling oaked? New oak is uncommon in Australian Riesling. Stainless-steel fermentation is more typical, although some producers use techniques such as lees ageing or alternative vessels to build texture. Can Riesling be aged? Some Rieslings age very well and can develop honeyed, nutty, toasty or lemon-curd characters. Many are also enjoyable young for their fresh citrus and floral character. For more foundational context, start with what is wine? or explore the grape varieties index.

title: What is rosé?
description: Rosé is a wine style, not a single grape or sweetness level. Learn how it gets its colour and how to choose, serve and enjoy it.
text: Highlights Rosé is a wine style with a colour ranging from pale pink and salmon to deeper pink and copper. It is usually made from red grapes, but with much less skin contact than red wine. Rosé is not defined by one grape, region, sweetness level or production method. It can be dry, off-dry or sweet, and pale colour does not automatically mean dry wine. Direct pressing, short skin contact and saignée are three ways to make rosé. Rosé is generally not made by mixing finished red and white wine. Australian rosé is made from many grape varieties and regions. Serve it chilled, then reseal and refrigerate any leftovers. Quick answer Rosé is a wine style known for its pink-to-copper colour and fresh, fruit-driven character. It is most commonly made from red grapes, but the juice spends only limited time with the grape skins. That brief contact gives the wine some colour without the extended extraction associated with most red wine. Rosé is therefore not a single grape variety or a synonym for a sweet wine. A bottle can be dry, off-dry or sweet; pale or deeply coloured; light-bodied or more structured; still or sparkling. The colour usually comes from controlled contact between juice and red grape skins. Winemakers may press the grapes quickly, leave the juice with the skins for a short time, or use a technique called saignée , in which some pink juice is drained from a red-wine ferment and fermented separately. The simplest way to understand rosé is this: it is usually made from red grapes, but handled so that the wine gets less colour and tannin from the skins than a typical red wine. How does rosé get its colour? Grape juice is not always deeply coloured simply because the grapes have dark skins. Much of the pigment that gives red wine its colour is extracted from the skins during winemaking. For rosé, the winemaker controls how much colour and structure are extracted. Less skin contact generally means less colour and less tannin, although grape variety, ripeness, temperature, pressing and other decisions also affect the result. That is why rosé can range from almost onion-skin or peach shades through salmon and bright pink to copper and deeper magenta. Colour can offer clues about how the wine was made, but it does not tell you everything about how it will taste. A pale rosé is not automatically sweeter, drier or better than a darker one. Colour, sweetness, acidity and body are related to winemaking, but they are not the same thing. Three common ways to make rosé Direct pressing With direct pressing , red grapes are pressed soon after arriving at the winery. The juice is separated from the skins early, so it takes on only a small amount of colour. This approach can produce a particularly delicate-looking rosé, but there is no universal colour or flavour outcome. The grape variety and the winemaker’s choices still matter. Short maceration Maceration means leaving juice or crushed grapes in contact with the skins so colour, flavour and phenolic compounds can be extracted. For rosé, that contact is limited. The winemaker separates the juice when the desired colour and structure have been reached. A little more contact may produce a deeper-coloured wine with more texture, but it does not create a fixed style every time. Saignée Saignée —French for “bleeding”—involves draining some pink-coloured juice from a tank of crushed red grapes. The removed juice can then be fermented separately as rosé. The technique is associated with a red-wine ferment, so saignée is not simply another name for all rosé production. Much rosé is made deliberately through direct pressing or short skin contact instead. Is rosé made by mixing red and white wine? Not as a general method. Most rosé is made by controlling colour extraction from grapes, usually red grapes, rather than by pouring finished red wine into finished white wine. Rules around blending differ between countries, wine categories and protected regional designations. Some sparkling-wine categories and regional specifications have their own provisions. It is therefore more accurate to say that red-and-white blending is not the standard explanation for rosé—not that it is universally illegal or that it never occurs in any category. The important beginner distinction is between blending and saignée . Saignée removes juice from a red-wine ferment before that juice is fermented separately. It is not the same as mixing finished red and white wines. Rosé compared with red and white wine Rosé and red wine are both commonly made from red grapes. The main difference is how long the juice remains with the skins. Red wine generally receives longer skin contact, extracting more colour and tannin. Rosé normally receives less, producing a paler wine with less tannic grip. White wine is commonly made by pressing grapes and fermenting the juice with little or no skin contact. Rosé may also be fermented as separated juice, but it usually has some colour and flavour influence from red grape skins. Rosé often shows fresh red-fruit notes such as strawberry, raspberry or cherry. Depending on the grape and winemaking, it may also suggest citrus, melon or flowers. Is rosé sweet? It can be—but it does not have to be. Rosé is made in dry, off-dry and sweet styles. Dry means the wine has little perceived sweetness, although acidity and fruit flavours influence how dry it feels. Sweetness is mainly affected by the amount of residual sugar left in the finished wine and by the balance between sugar and acidity. A pale rosé can be completely dry. A darker rosé can also be dry. If sweetness matters to you, check the label, producer notes or ask the person selling the wine rather than judging by colour. Australian rosé Australian rosé is not one regional or grape variety style. It is made across many regions from varieties including Shiraz, Grenache, Merlot, Nebbiolo and Pinot Noir, among others. That variety gives you a useful starting point when reading a label. A grape name can suggest the kind of fruit or structure you might encounter, but it is not a guarantee. Australian labels may include a grape variety, vintage or Geographical Indication, commonly called a GI , which identifies a wine-growing region. These details are optional rather than requirements for every bottle. Where a single variety, vintage or GI claim is made, Australian labelling rules apply, including the relevant 85 per cent threshold. How to serve and store rosé Chill still rosé before serving. In warm conditions, it may need time in the refrigerator or an ice bucket to reach a refreshing temperature. Avoid serving it so cold that its aroma and flavour disappear. After opening, reseal the bottle and refrigerate it. Still rosé is usually at its freshest over the next few days. Sparkling rosé loses its bubbles more quickly, so use a proper sparkling-wine stopper and drink it sooner. You do not need special glassware. A regular white-wine glass is a useful choice. What food goes with rosé? Rosé is a flexible partner at the table. Try it with salads and grilled vegetables, seafood and shellfish, grilled chicken, charcuterie, picnic foods, fresh or soft cheeses, tomato-based dishes and mildly spiced food. A dry, lively rosé may suit seafood and salads particularly well. A fuller or more deeply coloured example can stand up to grilled foods. Sweeter rosé may work with spicy dishes or fruit-based foods. These are starting points, not rules. In summary Rosé is a broad wine style, not a single grape, region or sweetness level. Its colour usually comes from limited contact between red grape juice and skins. Direct pressing, short maceration and saignée are different ways to achieve that style. Rosé can be dry or sweet, pale or deep, still or sparkling. When choosing one, use the label and producer description rather than assuming colour tells you everything. For the broader foundations, see What is wine? and How wine is made .

title: What is Sangiovese?
description: Sangiovese is an Italian red grape known for bright acidity, savoury character and red-fruit flavours. Learn what to expect in Australian examples.
text: title: What is Sangiovese? description: Sangiovese is an Italian red wine grape known for cherry flavours, lively acidity and noticeable tannin. Learn what Sangiovese wine tastes like and how styles vary. canonical: https://winedaddy.com.au/what-is-sangiovese/ article_type: Educational Guide What is Sangiovese? Highlights Sangiovese is an Italian red wine grape variety, not one single wine style. It is best known for dry red wines with cherry flavours, lively acidity and noticeable tannin. Plum, herbs, spice and savoury notes may also appear, depending on the wine. Chianti and Brunello di Montalcino are famous Sangiovese-based appellations, not definitions of every Sangiovese wine. Australian Sangiovese can be brighter, riper, darker or more savoury depending on its region and how it is made. Its acidity and tannin make it a natural partner for tomato-based dishes, pizza and grilled food. Quick answer Sangiovese is an Italian red wine grape variety strongly associated with Tuscany. It is used to make wines ranging from light and fresh to dark, firm and structured. A typical Sangiovese wine is dry, with flavours of cherry, sour cherry and other red fruits. It often has lively acidity, which gives the wine freshness and a mouth-watering quality, along with noticeable tannin that can feel drying or grippy. Sangiovese is not a fixed recipe. Climate, vineyard site, ripeness, harvest timing, extraction, oak, blending and maturation all influence the finished wine. That is why one bottle may taste bright and savoury while another is richer, darker and more powerful. The variety is famous in Italy through wines such as Chianti and Brunello di Montalcino, but it is also grown and made in Australia. Australian examples are produced in places including the King Valley, McLaren Vale, Riverina, Riverland and the Murray–Darling–Swan Hill area. What does Sangiovese taste like? Sangiovese commonly shows cherry, sour cherry, plum and other red-fruit flavours. Depending on the wine, you may also notice herbs, violet, spice, earth or savoury flavours. Its structure is often as important as its fruit. Acidity gives Sangiovese lift and freshness, while tannin provides grip and a drying sensation. Many examples are medium-bodied, although riper fruit, more extraction, oak maturation or blending can produce a fuller, more structured wine. The finish may be fresh, savoury, tannic or persistent. There is no single tasting profile that applies to every bottle. Is Sangiovese sweet? Most still Sangiovese is dry, meaning it contains little perceptible residual sugar. However, a wine can taste of ripe cherry or plum without being sweet. This is a useful distinction when reading a tasting note: fruitiness describes flavour and aroma; dryness describes sweetness on the palate . A dry Sangiovese can still taste generously fruity. Why does Sangiovese vary so much? The grape’s final style reflects a chain of decisions and conditions. Climate and site Warmer conditions can encourage riper fruit, darker flavours and a fuller impression. Cooler conditions or earlier harvesting may preserve brighter acidity and more red-fruit or herbal character. These are tendencies, not rules. Vineyard elevation, aspect, rainfall, water availability, the season and the producer’s decisions all matter too. A warm region does not automatically produce heavy wine, and a cool region does not automatically produce thin wine. Ripeness and harvest timing Riper grapes can contribute darker fruit, greater body and softer-feeling tannin. Earlier-picked grapes may retain more acidity and show fresher red-fruit flavours. Neither approach is automatically better. The winemaker is balancing freshness, ripeness, tannin and alcohol to create the intended style. Extraction, oak and maturation During red-wine making, contact with grape skins helps extract colour and tannin. More intensive extraction can create a darker, firmer wine, while gentler extraction may preserve freshness and make the wine feel lighter. Oak can add texture and flavours such as spice, toast or vanilla. These are winemaking influences, not inherent Sangiovese flavours. Bottle maturation may soften tannin and bring more savoury, earthy or dried-fruit character, although ageing outcomes vary from wine to wine. Sangiovese may be bottled on its own or blended with other grape varieties. Blending can alter colour, body, aroma, tannin and balance. Sangiovese, Chianti and Brunello One of the easiest ways to understand Sangiovese is to separate the grape from the wine category. Sangiovese is the grape variety. Chianti is a regulated Italian appellation whose wines contain 70% to 100% Sangiovese according to the Chianti consortium’s summary of the rules. Brunello di Montalcino is a specific appellation made exclusively from Sangiovese, locally called Brunello, under defined production and maturation rules. Chianti and Brunello therefore show different expressions of Sangiovese. They do not mean that every Sangiovese wine must taste like either one. Chianti is commonly described as dry, savoury and slightly tannic, with red-fruit and violet notes. Brunello di Montalcino is typically associated with a more robust, structured style and extended maturation. These are appellation-based traditions, not universal characteristics of the grape. Sangiovese in Australia Sangiovese is an established but relatively small variety in Australia. Wine Australia’s 2024 snapshot recorded 5,906 tonnes crushed in 2024. Its planting figure—438 hectares—uses 2015 Australian Bureau of Statistics data, so the two figures refer to different years. The largest regional shares listed in that snapshot included Murray–Darling–Swan Hill, the King Valley, Riverina, Riverland and McLaren Vale. These figures describe production context, not a ranking of quality. Australian Sangiovese is not one national style. Depending on the region, season, vineyard material and winemaking, it may be bright and cherry-driven, fuller and darker-fruited, or more savoury and structured. It can be useful to compare Australian and Italian examples, but neither country produces one uniform style. What food goes with Sangiovese? Sangiovese’s acidity can work particularly well with tomato-based foods, while its tannin and savoury character can suit roasted or grilled ingredients. Try it with: tomato-based pasta; pizza; grilled or roasted vegetables; roast or grilled meats; mushroom dishes; and other savoury Mediterranean-style foods. These are suggestions rather than rules. The best match depends on the wine’s weight, tannin and fruit character, as well as the dish. For serving, Sangiovese is generally more refreshing when served slightly cool rather than warm. A lighter, fresher bottle may suit a cooler serving temperature than a fuller, oak-matured example. How to choose a Sangiovese If you are buying Sangiovese for the first time, start by thinking about the style you enjoy: For freshness and red-fruit flavour, look for a lighter or more fruit-driven style. For structure and savoury depth, choose a wine described as firm, concentrated or oak-matured. If you are cooking with tomatoes, acidity is likely to be useful at the table. If you prefer softer wines, be aware that young Sangiovese can have noticeable tannin. The grape name gives you a helpful starting point, but the region, producer and winemaking details on the label can change the experience considerably. For more grape varieties, explore WineDaddy’s grape variety guide . For a broader introduction to wine, see what is wine? . Sangiovese FAQs Is Sangiovese a red or white grape? Sangiovese is a red wine grape variety. Is Sangiovese the same as Chianti? No. Sangiovese is the grape. Chianti is a regulated Italian wine appellation that uses Sangiovese as its principal grape. Is Brunello made from Sangiovese? Yes. Brunello di Montalcino is made exclusively from Sangiovese, which is locally called Brunello. Is Sangiovese full-bodied? It can be, but not every example is. Many Sangiovese wines are medium-bodied and fresh, while riper, more extracted or oak-matured examples may feel fuller and more structured. Is Sangiovese a good food wine? Often, yes. Its acidity and tannin can work well with tomato-based dishes, grilled food, roasted vegetables and savoury meats.

title: What Is Sauvignon Blanc?
description: Sauvignon Blanc is a fresh, aromatic white wine grape variety. Learn what it tastes like, whether it is sweet and how Australian styles vary.
text: Highlights Sauvignon Blanc is a white wine grape variety and the name commonly used for wines made from it. It is often fresh, aromatic and high in perceived acidity, with flavours such as citrus, grapefruit, passionfruit, herbs or grass. Most still Sauvignon Blanc is dry. Fruity or tropical flavours do not necessarily mean the wine contains much sugar. It is not always grassy, sweet, light-bodied or unoaked. Australian examples vary from crisp, aromatic wines to broader Sauvignon Blanc–Semillon blends. Serve it chilled and try it with seafood, salads, goat’s cheese or fresh, herb-led dishes. Quick Answer: What Is Sauvignon Blanc? Sauvignon Blanc is a white wine grape variety. The same name is also commonly used for wines made primarily from that grape. It is best known for producing fresh, aromatic white wines with noticeable acidity. Depending on where the grapes are grown and how the wine is made, you might taste lemon, lime, grapefruit, passionfruit, guava, gooseberry, freshly cut grass, herbs or green capsicum. Most still Sauvignon Blanc is made in a dry style. That does not mean it lacks fruit flavour. A wine can taste strongly of passionfruit or tropical fruit while containing little residual sugar. Fruitiness, sweetness, acidity and body are different parts of the wine. Sauvignon Blanc is often light to medium bodied, but it has a broad range of styles. Stainless-steel fermentation commonly produces a bright, direct and aromatic wine. Riper fruit, barrel fermentation, oak maturation, lees contact or blending with Semillon can create a fuller, rounder or more textural result. In Australia, Adelaide Hills offers one fresh, aromatic expression, while Margaret River is particularly associated with Sauvignon Blanc–Semillon blends ranging from crisp and herbal to richer and more oak-influenced. Tasmania is another useful cool-climate context. These are broad tendencies, not rules for every bottle. What Does Sauvignon Blanc Taste Like? Sauvignon Blanc’s flavour can be easier to understand by separating aroma, acidity, body and sweetness. Aroma and flavour Common descriptions include: lemon, lime and grapefruit; passionfruit and guava; gooseberry; tropical fruit; freshly cut grass; herbs; and green capsicum. Not every bottle shows all of these characters. Some are strongly citrus-driven, while others are tropical, herbal, savoury or more restrained. These descriptions are tasting comparisons, not ingredients added to the wine. Acidity Acidity gives wine freshness and lift. It can make your mouth water and leave the wine feeling lively rather than heavy. Sauvignon Blanc is commonly associated with noticeable acidity, although the impression changes with climate, ripeness, harvest timing and winemaking. Body and finish Body is the sense of weight or fullness in your mouth. Many Sauvignon Blancs are light to medium bodied, but riper fruit, oak, lees contact or Semillon blending can give the wine more breadth. The finish may be crisp and citrusy, herbal, tropical or softly textured. A fresh finish is one reason Sauvignon Blanc works well with lighter foods. Is Sauvignon Blanc Sweet? Usually, no. Most ordinary still Sauvignon Blanc is dry, meaning it contains little perceptible residual sugar. However, ripe fruit flavours can make a dry wine seem sweet. Passionfruit, guava and tropical fruit are aroma and flavour impressions; they are not proof that the wine contains much sugar. A useful way to think about it is: Dryness relates mainly to residual sugar. Fruitiness describes aromas and flavours. Acidity creates freshness and tension. Body describes weight and fullness. A Sauvignon Blanc can therefore be dry, fruity and high in acidity at the same time. Why Does Sauvignon Blanc Vary So Much? The grape responds clearly to both its growing conditions and the choices made in the winery. Climate and ripeness Cool but sunny conditions can help the grapes retain acidity while developing aromatic intensity. Warmer conditions may encourage riper, broader and more tropical flavours, although site, vintage and harvest decisions also matter. Harvest timing changes the balance of flavours. Earlier-picked grapes may retain sharper freshness and greener, herbaceous characters. Longer ripening can encourage riper fruit and reduce some vegetal notes. Winemakers may combine fruit picked at different stages of ripeness to create balance. Sauvignon Blanc can also produce vigorous foliage. Vineyard canopy management and light exposure can influence the balance between green, herbaceous character and riper fruit expression. Fermentation and maturation Stainless-steel fermentation is common. It helps winemakers preserve fresh aromas and a direct, crisp style. Oak is not mandatory, though. Barrel fermentation or oak maturation can add breadth, texture and richness. Lees contact can also contribute a rounder mouthfeel. Some wines are bottled relatively soon after fermentation for a fresh, immediate style. Others are given more time, oak influence or blending to develop a broader shape. Australian Sauvignon Blanc Styles Australia does not have one single Sauvignon Blanc flavour profile. The variety is grown in regions with different climates and is handled in different ways. Adelaide Hills Adelaide Hills is a prominent Australian context for Sauvignon Blanc. Wine Australia describes examples from the region as lively and aromatic, with grapefruit, tropical fruit and crisp acidity. This is a useful style to try if you enjoy fresh, fragrant white wines. Margaret River Margaret River provides a different illustration. Sauvignon Blanc is commonly blended with Semillon, which can add mid-palate weight and texture. Wines may range from light, crisp, lemony and herbal to fuller, more tropical and oak-influenced. This is why Sauvignon Blanc should not be assumed to mean only a lean, unoaked wine. Tasmania Tasmania is another cool-climate Australian context. It helps demonstrate how the variety can be grown in cooler settings where freshness and aromatic definition are important. Individual wines will still vary according to site, vintage and winemaking. A brief comparison with New Zealand can also be useful. New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc is often associated with pronounced passionfruit, grapefruit, grass and capsicum characters, but New Zealand itself produces a range of styles. It should not be treated as the only correct expression of the grape. How Should You Serve Sauvignon Blanc? Serve Sauvignon Blanc chilled or well chilled. An exact serving temperature is not necessary to enjoy a beginner bottle, and the ideal temperature can vary with the wine’s body and style. A very aromatic, light-bodied wine may feel particularly refreshing when well chilled. A fuller, oaked or Sauvignon Blanc–Semillon blend can show more of its texture if it is not served excessively cold. What Food Goes With Sauvignon Blanc? Its acidity and freshness make Sauvignon Blanc a natural partner for lighter, bright-flavoured dishes. Try it with: oysters and other shellfish; fresh white fish; salads; goat’s cheese; lightly prepared chicken or pork; dishes with citrus, herbs or garlic; and fresh vegetables. These are starting points, not rules. A crisp Sauvignon Blanc may suit a simple seafood dish, while a broader Margaret River blend may work better with richer fish, roast chicken or a creamy goat’s cheese preparation. How to Recognise the Style in Your Glass When tasting Sauvignon Blanc, ask four simple questions: What aromas stand out? Citrus, tropical fruit, herbs or green characters? How fresh does it feel? Notice the acidity and mouth-watering finish. How much weight does it have? Light and crisp, or broad and textured? Does it taste sweet, or merely fruity? A tropical aroma can still belong to a dry wine. The main lesson is that Sauvignon Blanc is a grape with a recognisable personality, not a single fixed recipe. It can be crisp, aromatic and herbal, or riper, fuller and more textured. Australian wines are well worth exploring across regions and styles. Related Learning What is wine?
